blockMcqs.question: What is the single biggest benefit of design patterns?
options: They run faster than hand-written code
A shared vocabulary that conveys a design fast
They remove the need for interfaces
They guarantee bug-free code
blockMcqs.explanation: Naming a shape lets a whole team discuss design in shorthand; the structure is secondary.

blockMcqs.question: Adding a new algorithm to a clean Strategy setup means:
options: Editing the context's switch statement
Writing one new class, touching nothing else
Subclassing every existing strategy
Changing the Strategy interface
blockMcqs.explanation: The context delegates through the interface, so existing code stays closed to modification.

blockMcqs.question: Why does Checkout take its strategy as a constructor argument?
options: To make the strategy a singleton
So it's injected and swappable, not hard-wired
To avoid defining an interface
So the strategy can read Checkout's fields
blockMcqs.explanation: Injecting it keeps Checkout decoupled from concrete classes and easy to test with fakes.

blockMcqs.question: In Observer, what does the subject know about its observers?
options: Their concrete classes and internal state
Only that they implement the observer interface
The order they must run in
Nothing — it broadcasts blindly to all objects
blockMcqs.explanation: This decoupling is the point: subscribers can be added or removed without touching the subject.

blockMcqs.question: Why can decorators be stacked in any combination?
options: Each subclasses the core object
They share the same interface as what they wrap
The runtime reorders them automatically
They mutate the inner object's type
blockMcqs.explanation: Sharing the interface lets a decorator wrap another decorator, composing features at runtime.

blockMcqs.question: Strategy and State share a shape. What distinguishes them?
options: State is faster than Strategy
Strategy uses inheritance, State uses composition
State objects drive transitions; clients pick strategies
Only Strategy needs an interface
blockMcqs.explanation: Same structure, different intent: who decides the next behavior is the dividing line.

blockMcqs.question: When should you reach for a pattern over plain direct code?
options: Always, to keep code consistent
When the second reason to vary actually arrives
Only on the first line of any module
Never, until an interview requires it
blockMcqs.explanation: YAGNI: indirection only pays off once the variation it flexes for is real.

blockMcqs.question: Why is Singleton considered dangerous?
options: It allocates too much memory
Its global access point hides dependencies and hurts testing
It can never be made thread-safe
It only works in functional languages
blockMcqs.explanation: The risk is the global reach, not the single instance; injecting one instance avoids it.
